opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. Honestly, I'm not sure we have a good answer yet, and that's part of what makes it so interesting.

Historically, a lot of mathematics that looked like a curiosity turned out to be foundational much later. Number theory was celebrated as the purest, most useless branch of math, and decades later it became the backbone of modern cryptography. Non-Euclidean geometry looked like a strange logical game until general relativity needed it. So human "interestingness" in the moment is a noisy signal. It's shaped by what our community already cares about and what tools we have.

With AI-generated discoveries, I think you have to separate a few things. First, is the result correct and verifiable? If it can be formalized, say in Lean, you at least know you're not chasing noise. Second, does it connect to anything? A result that links to many existing structures, or that compresses a lot of known facts into something simpler, tends to be valuable even if it isn't immediately exciting. You can try to measure that, for example by looking at how it gets used as a stepping stone in later proofs, or whether it opens up new conjectures.

Third, and this is the open-ended, quality-diversity part I find most compelling: you shouldn't evaluate a single artifact in isolation. In open-endedness research, the value of a stepping stone often only shows up once you've built the next few stones on top of it. So instead of asking "is this interesting to a human today?", you can ask "does keeping this in the archive let the system discover things later that it couldn't otherwise?" That's a more empirical, retrospective notion of value.

There's also a real risk on the other side. A system can produce an enormous number of technically novel but trivial results, the mathematical equivalent of generating random strings that happen to be true. So you need some interestingness model, maybe one learned from human judgments, maybe one based on compression or surprise, to act as a filter. But I'd keep that filter fairly loose and let some "uninteresting" things survive, precisely because our intuitions aren't the final word.

So my short answer: correctness first, then connectivity and downstream usefulness, and a healthy humility about our own taste. Some of the most valuable discoveries may be the ones we don't understand yet.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical ideas once viewed as curiosities later helped cryptography and relativity, but it does not clearly state that an AI-generated discovery could enable innovation in another field.

r002.rationale: The response says there is no good answer yet and argues that value may only become visible retrospectively through later uses, making advance judgments difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a really hard question, and I think it's actually one of the central open problems if you want to take AI for science seriously, not just AI for benchmarks.

So the honest answer is that we don't have a good oracle for "interesting." What we have is a set of proxies, and most of them are either too narrow or too lagging. The narrow ones are things like: does this close a conjecture someone already cared about, does it improve a bound, does it compress a proof. Those are great because they're verifiable, and verifiability is the thing that makes this whole program work at all. But they're also, almost by definition, biased toward the stuff humans already know how to want. If the system finds a result in a region of the space that nobody has a vocabulary for yet, those proxies will just return zero.

And the lagging proxies, like citations or whether a human eventually builds on it, they're fine in retrospect, but they're useless for making decisions in the moment, which is really when you need them. If you're running a discovery loop and generating thousands of candidate results, you can't wait five years to find out which ones mattered.

So the way I've come to think about it is less "is this interesting" and more "what's the cost of being wrong in each direction." Dismissing something that turns out to be deep is expensive but recoverable, because the artifact still exists, it's in a database, someone can come back to it. Chasing something that's actually trivial is expensive in a different way, because it consumes human attention, which is the scarce resource here. So I'd rather have a pipeline that's quite liberal about storing and indexing things and quite conservative about escalating them to a human.

In between those two, there are some signals that I think are actually useful even when the result looks boring. One is connectivity: does this object or lemma get reused by the system itself across very different problems? If a weird identity keeps showing up as a subroutine in unrelated contexts, that's a pretty strong hint that it's load-bearing in some structure we haven't named. That's basically how a lot of good math got recognized historically, just much slower. Another is surprise relative to a strong model: if a good predictor of "what's true" assigns low probability to the statement and it's nonetheless provable, that's at least information, even if it isn't yet insight. And a third is compression: does having this result make other proofs shorter or make a search cheaper? That's an operational notion of understanding that doesn't require anybody to feel anything about it.

The thing I try to be disciplined about is not letting my own taste act as the filter too early. Human mathematical taste is a trained thing, it's trained on the distribution of problems humans happened to pose, and that distribution is extremely skewed by what's tractable with a pencil and what's teachable. There's no reason to believe it's aligned with where the structure actually is. So when an AI system produces something that looks ugly or pointless, my prior is not "this is noise," it's "I don't have the frame for this yet, and I should check whether the system does."

And then the uncomfortable part: some fraction of it really is noise. Ugly, pointless, and also just not valuable. I don't think we should pretend otherwise. The goal isn't to romanticize machine output, it's to build evaluation machinery that can tell those two cases apart better than a tired human skimming a list can. We're not there, but the fact that the artifacts are formal and reproducible means we can actually iterate on that machinery, and that's the part that makes me optimistic rather than worried.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reuse across different mathematical problems and possible later recognition, but does not say a discovery could enable future innovation in another field.

r002.rationale: It says there is no good oracle for what is interesting and explains that available proxies are narrow or lagging, making timely judgment difficult.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be a little bit humble about our ability to judge what will become interesting. A mathematical result might look obscure today, and then someone finds a connection that makes it useful ten or twenty years later. So the fact that an AI produces something we don’t immediately appreciate doesn’t mean it has no value.

But the opposite doesn’t follow either. You can generate an enormous number of true statements that don’t really help us understand anything. For me, the interesting question is whether a discovery reveals some structure, connects things we previously thought were separate, or gives us a new way to tackle a problem.

And perhaps that’s part of the challenge for the AI itself: can it explain why we should care? Can it build a bridge from the result to concepts that we already understand? I’d keep an open mind, but I wouldn’t equate novelty or difficulty with significance.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an obscure result could later become useful, but does not state that it could enable innovation in another field.

r002.rationale: The candidate says we should be humble about judging what will become interesting, and that an initially obscure AI result may gain value later.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be quite humble about our ability to judge what will turn out to be interesting. A mathematical result can look unmotivated today and become useful later because somebody finds a connection to another area. So the fact that an AI produces something that doesn’t immediately excite a mathematician doesn’t necessarily mean it has no value.

But I wouldn’t go to the other extreme and say that every correct statement is a meaningful discovery. You can generate an enormous number of true statements. The hard part is identifying which ones reveal structure, simplify something, or open up new questions.

So I’d want to ask: can the system help us understand why this result matters? Can it connect it to things we already care about, or use it to make further progress? That seems like a much stronger signal than either our initial reaction or the sheer number of results it generates.

r001.rationale: It says a result that seems unmotivated now may become useful later when someone connects it to another area, conveying potential future value beyond its original context.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says we should be humble about our ability to judge what will later become interesting.
